content.title: Alabama coach: Michigan’s front line as good as any in recent college basketball history
content.text: Wolverines BasketballPublished: Mar. 26, 2026, 3:42 p.m.Alabama Crimson Tide head coach Nate Oats during practice day before the Sweet 16 at United Center in Chicago, Ill. on Thursday, March 26 2026.MLive.comBy Andrew Kahn | akahn1@mlive.comCHICAGO — Nate Oats knows all about Yaxel Lendeborg. The two were less than 60 miles apart last season, with Oats coaching Alabama and Lendeborg spending his final year at UAB. Lendeborg is now in his lone season at Michigan and one of the best players in the country.“You’re going to have to hope he misses some shots because he’s a super athletic basketball player with a lot of size,” Oats said.Lendeborg is the key piece for a Michigan team that plays Alabama in Friday’s Sweet 16 (7:35 p.m. ET, TBS).Oats, being in-state, made some calls once Lendeborg entered the portal. They didn’t go very far. At that point other schools, including Michigan, were further along and had deeper pockets. “We didn’t spend a lot of time on it,” Oats said, but he knew the talent Michigan was getting.If Lendeborg is at the small forward spot, as he is in Michigan’s starting lineup, he’s too tall and powerful for the average defender. At the power forward spot, he’s probably too fast.“So you’re going to have to guard him with guys that are big enough, strong enough, and athletic enough,” Oats said. “And there’s not many of those so you’re going to have to get some help from teammates on the floor.”That’s true with most of Michigan’s players. Alabama’s defense has been far from elite this season. “This is not a game where you can guard a lot of these guys one-on-one because you’re going to lose the one-on-one,” Oats said.Relationship with MayOats and May have history. Oats was at Romulus (Michigan) High School when May was an assistant at nearby Eastern Michigan and they struck up a friendship then.At Romulus, many college coaches came through the doors. Some were just trying to use the coach to get the players. Others were interested in a genuine relationship. “Dusty was one of those guys that was genuine, real, smart, and worked hard,” Oats said.They’ve stayed in touch since.“I think he’s one of the best coaches in college basketball,” Oats said. “It’s not one of these games where we’re going in and they’ve got a lot of talent and we think we can just out-coach a poorly-coached talented team. Michigan is very talented and very well-coached.”Facing No. 1Alabama reached the Elite Eight last year, the Final Four the year before, and was the Tournament’s No. 1 overall seed the year before that. Oats knows March Madness success and thinks his program can win it all, if not now then in the near future.Beating this Michigan team, though, this year, will take a special effort.“Michigan is a different deal,” he said. “I mean, they’re physically imposing. There’s not too many holes on Michigan’s team. Their front line is as good as any front line in college basketball in recent history. Their backcourt is very good.”The Crimson Tide take and make enough 3s to scare anyone. They’re a 4 seed for a reason, despite their two comfortable wins to the start this event. Michigan has found many ways to win. Alabama has allowed at least 90 points in six of its nine losses.“We’re going to have to make some shots,” Oats said. “We’re going to have to take care of the ball. We’re going to have to find a way to rebound.
